walkthroughs.body_html:
Foundations of Environmental Systems — a core area of Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Foundations of Environmental Systems brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Foundations of Environmental Systems.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Why are top predators most affected by persistent pollutants like mercury?
options: Predators have weaker immune systems.
Biomagnification concentrates pollutants at each trophic level up the food chain.
Because polar bears help spread heat.
Predators are exposed to more pollution directly.

mcqs.q: Why is ice-albedo feedback a positive feedback loop?
options: Because polar bears help spread heat.
Less ice means less reflective surface, so more sunlight is absorbed, causing more warming and more melting.
Predators have weaker immune systems.
Because warming is positive (a good thing).
Water bubbling up from underground.
Water vapour released from plant leaves to the atmosphere.
Water flowing through soil into rivers.
Because polar bears help spread heat.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Earth Summit”?
options: Meeting present needs without compromising ability of future generations to meet theirs (Brundtland 1987).
1992 Rio Conference produced Agenda 21, UNFCCC and CBD; landmark in environmental governance.
Analysing environment as interlinked open systems with inputs, outputs, flows, feedbacks.
Individual rational use of shared resource leads to collective ruin (Hardin 1968 in Science).
